title: Pharmaceutical Microbiology and Sterile Products
description: Microbial contamination of medicines, preservatives, sterilisation of pharmaceuticals, aseptic processing, sterility testing and antimicrobial assays.

topics.title: Microbial Contamination of Pharmaceuticals
topics.summary: Sources of contamination, spoilage, microbial limits and consequences.

notes.b: Medicines can be contaminated from raw materials (especially natural products such as starch, gums, herbal materials and water), water systems, the manufacturing environment, equipment, personnel (the largest source in cleanrooms — skin scales, hair), packaging and, after opening, during use. Contamination may cause infection (e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa in eye drops causing corneal ulcers; contaminated infusions causing septicaemia), spoilage (gas, discolouration, odour, loss of potency, emulsion cracking) and toxic metabolites. Water is the commonest source of Gram-negative contamination and endotoxins.
k: Pseudomonas in eye drops → corneal ulcers

notes.b: Pharmacopoeias set microbial limits for non-sterile products (total aerobic microbial count, total yeasts and moulds, and absence of specified organisms such as E. coli in oral products, Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa in topical products, Salmonella in some natural products). Sterile products (injections, eye preparations, irrigation fluids) must be free of viable microorganisms and, for parenterals, free of pyrogens (bacterial endotoxins). Water for injections is produced by distillation or equivalent and tested for endotoxin.
k: Non-sterile: limits + absence of specified pathogens
Water for injections tested for endotoxin

topics.title: Preservatives and Their Evaluation
topics.summary: Ideal properties, common preservatives, factors affecting activity and preservative efficacy testing.

notes.b: Preservatives are added to multi-dose and aqueous non-sterile preparations to prevent growth of contaminating microbes. Ideal properties: broad spectrum, effective at low concentration, non-toxic and non-irritant, stable, compatible and without odour or taste. Common preservatives: parabens (methyl- and propylparaben — oral and topical), benzalkonium chloride (a quaternary ammonium compound — eye drops), chlorhexidine, phenol and cresol (injections, e.g. insulin vials), benzyl alcohol, sorbic acid and benzoic acid/sodium benzoate (active in acidic pH, un-ionised form), thiomersal (vaccines) and alcohol (elixirs).
k: Benzoic and sorbic acid: need acidic pH

notes.b: Preservative activity is reduced by binding to macromolecules (e.g. parabens bind non-ionic surfactants like polysorbates), partitioning into the oil phase of emulsions, adsorption onto containers and rubber closures, unsuitable pH (weak acid preservatives work only in their un-ionised form at low pH), high microbial load and dilution. The preservative efficacy test (challenge test) inoculates the product with defined organisms (e.g. S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, E. coli, Candida albicans, Aspergillus brasiliensis) and measures log reduction over 28 days against pharmacopoeial criteria.
k: Challenge test: inoculate and count over 28 days

topics.title: Sterilisation of Pharmaceutical Products
topics.summary: Methods, D-value and Z-value, sterility assurance level and validation.

notes.b: Microbial death under a sterilising process follows first-order kinetics. The D-value (decimal reduction time) is the time at a given temperature to reduce the microbial population by 90% (one log). The Z-value is the temperature change needed to change the D-value tenfold. The F0 value expresses the lethality of a moist-heat process as equivalent minutes at 121 °C. Sterility is defined probabilistically: a sterility assurance level (SAL) of 10⁻⁶ means no more than a one-in-a-million chance of a non-sterile unit. Terminal sterilisation in the final container is preferred to aseptic processing.

Moist heat (autoclave, 121 °C for 15 min) for aqueous solutions in sealed containers and dressings; dry heat (160–180 °C) for glassware, oils and powders, and depyrogenation at ~250 °C; ethylene oxide gas for heat-sensitive devices (toxic, needs aeration); gamma irradiation for disposables and some raw materials; membrane filtration (0.22 µm) for heat-labile solutions (not terminal — requires aseptic filling; does not remove endotoxins or viruses reliably). Validation uses physical monitoring (temperature, pressure, time), chemical indicators and biological indicators: Geobacillus stearothermophilus spores for moist heat, Bacillus atrophaeus for dry heat and ethylene oxide, Bacillus pumilus for radiation, and Brevundimonas diminuta for filter challenge.
k: BIs: G. stearothermophilus (moist heat), B. atrophaeus (dry heat/EO)

topics.title: Aseptic Processing and Sterility Testing
topics.summary: Cleanroom grades, HEPA filtration, laminar airflow, gowning, media fills and sterility tests.

notes.b: Aseptic processing assembles pre-sterilised components in a controlled environment when terminal sterilisation is not possible. Cleanrooms are classified by particle counts (EU GMP grades A–D; ISO 5–8): Grade A (ISO 5) is the critical zone for filling and open operations, usually under unidirectional (laminar) airflow through HEPA filters (retaining ≥ 99.97% of 0.3 µm particles), within a Grade B background. Positive pressure cascades, airlocks, validated gowning, restricted personnel movement and environmental monitoring (settle plates, contact plates, active air sampling) are essential. Process simulation (media fill) replaces product with sterile growth medium to validate aseptic technique; contamination rate must be extremely low.
k: Grade A (ISO 5) critical zone under laminar flow

notes.b: The pharmacopoeial sterility test uses membrane filtration (preferred, especially for antimicrobial products — the membrane is rinsed to remove inhibitory substances) or direct inoculation into fluid thioglycollate medium (for anaerobes and aerobes, 30–35 °C) and soybean–casein digest medium (for aerobes and fungi, 20–25 °C), incubated for 14 days. Because it samples only a few units, it has limited statistical power and cannot prove sterility — assurance relies on validated processes. Bacterial endotoxins are detected by the Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) test (gel clot, turbidimetric or chromogenic), which has largely replaced the rabbit pyrogen test.
k: Sterility test: FTM and SCDM, 14 days
Test has limited power — rely on validation

topics.title: Antimicrobial Assays and Disinfectant Evaluation
topics.summary: MIC and susceptibility testing, microbiological assay of antibiotics and evaluation of disinfectants.

notes.b: The minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) is the lowest concentration of an antimicrobial that prevents visible growth (broth or agar dilution); the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) is the lowest concentration killing ≥ 99.9% of the inoculum. The Kirby–Bauer disc diffusion method measures zones of inhibition interpreted against CLSI/EUCAST breakpoints; the E-test gives an MIC on agar. Microbiological (bio)assays measure antibiotic potency by comparing zones of inhibition (cylinder-plate/cup-plate method) or turbidity produced by the test sample and a reference standard — used when chemical assays do not reflect biological activity (e.g. neomycin, gentamicin complexes).
k: Bioassay compares sample with a standard

notes.b: Disinfectant activity depends on concentration (concentration exponent — high for phenols, so dilution greatly reduces activity), contact time, temperature, pH, organic load (blood and pus inactivate chlorine and quaternary ammonium compounds) and the type of organism (prions > bacterial spores > mycobacteria > non-enveloped viruses > fungi > vegetative bacteria > enveloped viruses in resistance). Historical tests include the Rideal–Walker and Chick–Martin phenol coefficient tests; modern tests include suspension tests (European Standards, e.g. EN 1276) and surface tests, plus in-use (Kelsey–Sykes/capacity) tests.
k: Organic load inactivates chlorine and QACs
